posts.title: Three days to hang eleven paintings
posts.excerpt: Eleven paintings, three long days, and a room that kept asking for fewer works rather than more.
posts.content:
We started with sixteen paintings leaning against the walls of Room one. By the second evening there were eleven, and the room was quieter for it.

Daichi Morimoto and I hang by eye first and by tape measure second. Each painting sits with its centre at 148 centimetres, a little lower than most galleries, because his canvases are meant to be met straight on, not looked up to.

“The wall between two paintings is part of both of them.” — Daichi Morimoto

On the third day we moved one small painting to the end wall of Room two, alone. It is the first thing many visitors now photograph.

posts.title: A morning by the river with Yuna Takase
posts.excerpt: She draws beside the water, one sheet per sitting, and stops when the light on the river changes.
posts.content:
Yuna Takase works in a borrowed room above a boat shed, but most drawings are made outside, on a board on her knees, a few metres from the water.

She dilutes the ink until it is barely grey, then waits. A sheet is finished when the light on the river changes, sometimes after ten minutes, sometimes after two hours.

We chose twenty-four sheets for Slow Water, opening in November. She wanted forty. We will meet in the middle on the wall.

posts.title: Why the walls are painted white again after every show
posts.excerpt: Every exhibition leaves a shadow on the wall. The closing week is for painting it out.
posts.content:
When a painting comes down after eight weeks, it leaves a faint rectangle behind: a cleaner wall where the frame kept the dust and the light away. We call it the kage, the shadow, and it is where the gallery's name came from.

In the closing week we fill every nail hole, sand the patches and paint each wall twice in the same warm white. The new exhibition should never meet the ghost of the last one.

posts.title: Notes on a standing form
posts.excerpt: Haruki Oda carves small figures from offcuts of pale stone. Each one takes most of a year.
posts.content:
Haruki Oda's stone comes from a closed quarry yard: offcuts nobody wanted, too small for building. He keeps them for a year before he starts, turning them so the weather works on each side.

The form shown here is about sixty centimetres tall. In Stillness, Held it will stand alone in the small room, with one bench and nothing on the walls.

posts.title: The busiest quiet evening we have had
posts.excerpt: Two hundred people came to see nine shades of grey, and the room stayed almost silent.
posts.content:
Openings here are simple: the door stays open from six to eight, there is tea, and nobody gives a speech. For Grey Is a Colour about two hundred people came, many of them neighbours who had walked past for years.

What stayed with me was the sound. With so many people the room should have been loud, but it was mostly the floor, coats and the occasional whisper. The paintings asked for it.

posts.title: Why Mio Kanzaki paints the same three cups
posts.excerpt: Plain cups and jars, painted for months, until they stop being cups and start being light.
posts.content:
Mio Kanzaki has painted the same three vessels for six years: a tall jar, a cup without a handle and a small bowl. She moves them a few centimetres at a time.

She says the vessels are an excuse. What she is really painting is the morning light across the ledge, and how it is never the same twice. In March we hung eight of these paintings in a single line, and many visitors walked the line twice.
